rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5.1 - author's own 2007 data from Watermark sensors at 12 and 24 in. at 10 sites in a 4.4 acre clay-dominated vineyard, correlated with pressure-chamber leaf water potential (43 points, Fig. 3). Q2: Section 4 (Vineyard) and 5.1 - under SWT-based modified regulated deficit irrigation the 2007 yield reached a record 3.97 t/acre and Brix peaked at 26.5-28; author states the season's success in yield and ripeness supports the SWT-managed RDI approach; 24 in. SWT correlated with midday LWP (R2=0.42). Q4: Section 4 (Leaf Water Potential Measurements) and 5.1 - midday leaf water potential (vine water stress, the intermediate between sensed soil tension and grape yield/quality) was measured with a pressure chamber on the same 10 vines and used to set the 24 in. soil moisture target. Q7: Abstract and 5.1 - the usefulness of SWT depends on sampling sufficiently (2-3 sites/acre) and at appropriate depth: 24 in. correlated with LWP, 12 in. showed no correlation; minimum 2 h irrigation duration needed because of pressure transients. Q8: Section 5.1 - author states the yield/ripeness support for the approach is only indirect because many confounding factors affect yield; also two outlier points removed and 43-point sample.
rows.notes: Evidence on crop production is observational and uncontrolled (single vineyard, single season, no comparison treatment; vines in second production year so yield increase partly reflects vine age). The core own result is the SWT-LWP correlation; yield/quality outcomes are reported descriptively. Q6 answered no because the 4.4 acre vineyard is effectively a single field even though divided into irrigation blocks. Only R2 reported, no dispersion measure.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5.1 - author's own sensor network and pressure-chamber data from the 2007 season. Q2: Section 4 (Irrigation Paradigm) and 5.1 - irrigation in 2007 totalled 34 gal/vine, 26% less than the 46 gal/vine of 2006, with irrigation delayed until a higher stress threshold and intervals lengthened using real-time soil moisture at 24 in.; author lists reduced water consumption among the benefits of the SWT-managed approach. Q4: Section 5.1 - the study measures soil tension at 12 and 24 in. (wetting delay and drying transients) and midday LWP, the variables through which irrigation durations/intervals were set and lengthened to reduce water use. Q7: Abstract and 5.1 - SWT only useful when sampled sufficiently and at appropriate depth (24 in., not 12 in.); interval lengthening to save water was conditional on spot-checked LWP not dropping beyond about -15 bar, otherwise extra water was bought.
rows.notes: Water saving is an uncontrolled year-to-year comparison (2007 vs 2006) confounded by a very dry winter (16 in. vs 40 in. rain) and water scarcity that forced trucking of water; no control treatment. The explicit limitation statement in 5.1 refers to confounding factors affecting yield, not water use, so Q8 answered no with doubt. Q6 no: single 4.4 acre vineyard. No dispersion measures reported.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Grey-literature conference paper by a vineyard owner reporting a single-season, single-vineyard case study with a 43-point SWT vs leaf water potential correlation; crop production and water-saving outcomes are descriptive and uncontrolled. The review's 150 kPa at 60 cm criterion is not stated as such in the text, although the 24 in. (60 cm) depth and -13 bar LWP threshold are.
